title: MCQ elimination checklist
summary: A cross-topic decision tree for eliminating bad options before you fully solve the question.
why: The bank repeatedly rewards fast shape-checking: type, mutation, labels vs positions, parse vs format, and whether code actually returns/prints what the stem asks.

title: Mutation vs return value
summary: A single place to remember which operations change an object, which return a new value, and which return `None`.
why: A large share of wrong options fail because the code forgets that strings are immutable, that `append`/`sort`/`shuffle` mutate in place, or that some expressions return `None`.

title: Both / neither / all-of-the-above patterns
summary: How to handle options like Both / Neither / All of the given options without getting baited.
why: Many questions are not about syntax alone; they are about evaluating multiple candidate fragments independently, then translating that into the meta-option.

title: Types, None, bool, equality
summary: Core Python value semantics: types, `None`, truth values, and equality between strings, ints, floats, and booleans.
why: Basic-looking MCQs often hide one decisive fact: `'3' != 3`, `3 == 3.0`, empty containers are falsey, and reaching the end of a function returns `None`.

title: Membership and condition logic
summary: How `in`, `not in`, `and`, `or`, and `not` are used in the bank’s condition questions.
why: Several questions are solved by recognizing that membership is checked against the right object, and that condition precedence can make a nearly-correct answer wrong.

title: Built-ins and what they return
summary: High-yield built-ins that recur in output questions: what they take, what they return, and their usual type.
why: A surprising number of MCQs are really about remembering one built-in exactly: `len`, `sorted`, `sum`, `max`, `ord`, `type`, `count`, `index`.

title: Nested indexing and negative indices
summary: Read nested sequences quickly and avoid off-by-one errors with negative indices.
why: Several “easy” questions are solved by correctly evaluating expressions like `x[0][1]`, `x[-3][0]`, or by knowing exactly what `-1` and `-2` mean.

title: Slicing patterns
summary: How to read and write slices, especially when the exam asks for every nth element or reverse-order patterns.
why: Slice blanks and list-construction questions are common, and the distractors usually differ by one subtle issue: start, stop, step, or stop-exclusivity.

title: Loop templates
summary: Minimal patterns for range-based loops, while-loops, and loops with a carry variable such as `previous`.
why: The loop questions are rarely deep; they reward knowing a few exact templates and noticing inclusive vs exclusive bounds.

title: zip() and enumerate() core patterns
summary: The exact shapes of `zip()` and `enumerate()` and how they are used to build dictionaries and paired outputs.
why: These two functions recur in list, dict, and output questions. Students often mix up index/value order or forget that `enumerate(..., start=1)` shifts numbering.

title: List selection and aggregation
summary: Patterns for filtering lists, keeping elements that meet an index-based rule, or selecting one sub-list by a derived statistic.
why: The bank includes questions where the real task is not syntax but choosing the right selection criterion: equal to index, largest sum, or another derived property.

title: return, None, and function end
summary: Remember what `return` does, what happens without `return`, and why `return some_mutating_method(...)` is often wrong.
why: Questions on missing `return` and accidental `None` are everywhere, especially in function-definition items.

title: Local vs global scope
summary: How names live inside and outside functions, plus the classic shadowing and NameError traps.
why: Scope questions recur in almost every exam family: a local variable is used outside its function, or assignment inside a function makes Python treat the name as local.

title: Defaults and keyword arguments
summary: How default parameters work, when an argument becomes optional, and how keyword calls are matched.
why: Questions often hide the whole answer in one tiny detail: a default makes the second argument optional, or a keyword call binds by name instead of position.

title: *args and **kwargs
summary: The shapes of `*args` and `**kwargs`, and the common tasks the exams build around them.
why: Flexible-argument questions recur: sum keyword values, compute multiple outputs from any number of integers, or iterate over keyword names in insertion order.

title: Higher-order functions and lambda
summary: Lambda syntax, list-of-lambdas, and functions that receive another function plus values.
why: Lambda questions are usually short but high-yield: once you know the call shape, they become free points.

title: Imports and aliases
summary: Exact name rules for `import`, `from ... import ...`, and aliases.
why: Import questions are easy to lose for a silly reason: you imported under one name but used another.

title: split(), join(), replace()
summary: The three most exam-relevant string methods: split into parts, join parts back, and replace text.
why: These methods power URL/email/phone parsing, sentence shuffling, capitalization fixes, and many distractors.

title: find(), index(), count()
summary: Search-like string methods: where something starts, how many times it occurs, and when you get `-1` versus an error.
why: The bank uses these methods directly and also hides them inside “replace only the second occurrence” questions.

title: Case methods and capitalization
summary: The case methods that appear most often: `lower`, `upper`, `islower`, `isupper`, and `capitalize`.
why: Case conversion appears in list comprehensions, proper-noun cleanup, and string-validation distractors.

title: f-strings and .format()
summary: String formatting patterns that actually show up in the bank: f-strings, positional `.format`, and named placeholders.
why: Formatting questions are usually won by reading placeholders carefully and spotting spelling/placeholder mismatches.

title: Targeted string edits
summary: Small but common string-edit tasks: swap two marked letters, replace only one occurrence, or normalize text before comparison.
why: These questions reward knowing the exact order of operations, especially because strings are immutable and `replace(..., count)` works left-to-right.

title: URL, email, and phone parsing
summary: Reusable parsing pipelines for URLs, email addresses, and phone numbers.
why: The exam likes “extract piece X from string Y” questions. They are easiest when you think in short pipelines.

title: Build, count, and aggregate dictionaries
summary: How to build dictionaries from lists, count frequencies, and aggregate values from a dictionary.
why: Dictionary construction and counting are a core pre-midterm pattern that still shows up in finals and resits.

title: Dictionary iteration and equality
summary: The dict facts that exam setters love: equality ignores order, direct iteration yields keys, and `.values()` / `.items()` matter.
why: This is one of the most repeated distractor families in the bank.

title: Running totals and next-link dictionaries
summary: Two recurring dict-construction tasks: cumulative totals and linking each item to the next item.
why: These are a little more “algorithmic” than the average MCQ, so having the exact templates saves space and time.

title: List comprehension patterns
summary: The two list-comprehension forms you actually need: filter-only and map-with-conditional-expression.
why: These appear repeatedly and are easy to compress into one mental template.

title: Dictionary comprehension patterns
summary: Short templates for building dictionaries with comprehensions, plus the few transformations that recur in the bank.
why: This is one of the most repeated patterns across the exams.

title: Set vs list vs dict
summary: When to use a set, and how set behavior differs from lists and dicts in the kinds of MCQs this course uses.
why: A few deceptively simple options rely on knowing that sets remove duplicates and that dict membership checks keys, not values.

title: __init__, self, defaults, attributes
summary: Constructor essentials: `__init__`, `self`, default attributes, and what must be assigned onto the instance.
why: The most repeated OOP pattern in the bank is a class definition where one option forgets `self`, forgets a default, or forgets to save attributes on the instance.

title: Object state and collection attributes
summary: How objects store changing state, especially lists such as reviews or stored child objects like cars in a garage.
why: Many class questions are about an internal list attribute that grows over time, or capacity/state logic that depends on it.

title: Method calls and self
summary: Define methods with `self`, call them on the object, and do not pass `self` again manually.
why: A classic exam trap is an otherwise-correct method call that passes the object twice.

title: Compare/report method patterns
summary: How the bank writes comparison/report methods: use helper methods, compare object state carefully, then return a title/string/report.
why: These are common ‘long OOP’ questions. Once you see the pattern, they become template filling rather than full problem solving.

title: strptime() and strftime()
summary: The parse/format split, plus the directive patterns that recur throughout the exams.
why: Datetime questions often look harder than they are; most boil down to one directive string and knowing whether you are parsing or formatting.

title: Build datetimes from parts
summary: Build a full datetime from separate date parts, or from a date string plus a time string.
why: This shows up in both OOP and pandas questions where day/month/year or hour/minute arrive separately.

title: timedelta and day counts
summary: Use `timedelta` for shifting datetimes and `.days` for whole-day differences.
why: This snippet covers day-of-year, day differences, one-week jumps, and inclusive counting questions.

title: Overlap logic
summary: The overlap rule for meetings/events and the common string-vs-datetime mistakes around it.
why: Meeting/lunch-overlap questions recur and are surprisingly template-like.

title: Date sequences
summary: How to generate weekly date series, keep them computable, and only format them at the end.
why: The bank uses both list-based and DataFrame-based weekly-date generation tasks.

title: Series vs DataFrame
summary: The shape difference between selecting one column as a Series and selecting one-column DataFrame slices.
why: Several pandas questions are solved instantly once you know whether an option returns a Series or a DataFrame.

title: loc vs iloc
summary: Use `loc` for labels and `iloc` for integer positions. This single distinction solves many pandas MCQs.
why: The exams repeatedly mix DataFrames with row labels starting at 1 and positional indexing starting at 0.

title: Boolean masks and indexing
summary: Filter rows with boolean conditions and combine conditions safely.
why: This is one of the highest-frequency pandas skills in the bank.

title: Vectorized new columns
summary: Create new columns with vectorized column arithmetic instead of row-by-row Python loops where possible.
why: Many pandas questions are easiest because the answer is just `df['new'] = df['A'] - df['B']` or a similar vectorized expression.

title: map() vs apply()
summary: When to use `Series.map(...)` and when to use `DataFrame.apply(..., axis=1)`.
why: This is the main pandas trap family: elementwise vs rowwise reasoning.

title: String/date columns
summary: Common column transforms on strings and dates: abbreviations, suffixes, replacements, and building date strings.
why: These questions look varied but collapse to a few short patterns.

title: Build DataFrames from arguments
summary: Build a DataFrame from flexible arguments by collecting one list per column and passing them into `pd.DataFrame(...)`.
why: The email-address question is a pure template once you know the shape.

title: sort_index() vs sort_values()
summary: Choose `sort_index` when ordering by labels and `sort_values` when ordering by column contents.
why: Several pandas reverse-engineering questions depend on this distinction.
